nameStory: Coriander gets its name from the Greek word 'koriandron,' which may come from 'koris' meaning bedbug - some people thought the leaves smelled like these unwelcome insects! Interestingly, the fresh leaves are called cilantro (from Spanish) in the United States, while the seeds keep the name coriander everywhere.
description: Coriander is an annual herb in the carrot family that you might know better as cilantro when fresh. This Mediterranean native grows as a bushy plant with delicate, lacy leaves that become more finely divided as they mature. The plant typically reaches 1-2 feet tall and produces small white or pale pink flowers in umbrella-shaped clusters, eventually forming round, fragrant seeds.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lower leaves are broad and lobed like flat parsley, while upper leaves become feathery and thread-like. Crush a leaf and smell - it has a distinctive fresh, citrusy scent that some people love and others find soapy.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white or pale pink flowers cluster in flat-topped umbels (like tiny umbrellas) typical of the carrot family. Each flower has 5 petals and blooms in summer.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Round, ridged seeds about the size of peppercorns start green and turn tan-brown when ripe. They smell warm and spicy when crushed, completely different from the leaves.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as an upright, branching annual herb with a taproot. The plant has a delicate, airy appearance especially when the upper feathery leaves develop.

habitat: In New England, coriander is primarily found as a garden escape or in cultivated areas rather than truly wild habitats. Look for it in disturbed soils, compost areas, or near gardens where seeds may have been scattered. It prefers well-drained, fertile soil in sunny locations.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate and young plants emerge with their characteristic broad, parsley-like lower leaves. This is when the foliage is most tender and aromatic.
seasonality.summer: Plants flower with their distinctive white umbels and begin forming seeds. The leaves become more feathery and the plant reaches full height.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen to brown and the plant begins to die back. Ripe seeds can be collected and have their characteristic spicy aroma.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants have died, but seeds may persist in the soil to germinate the following spring.

funFact: Whether you love or hate cilantro isn't just personal preference - it's actually genetic! Variations in a specific gene called OR6A2 make some people taste soap or rottenness instead of the fresh, citrusy flavor that others enjoy.
confusionNotes: Young coriander plants look remarkably similar to flat-leaf parsley, but the smell test never fails - crush a leaf and coriander's distinctive citrusy scent (or soapy smell for some people) is unmistakable compared to parsley's mild, grassy aroma.
contextualKnowledge: This plant demonstrates how the same species can have completely different common names for different parts - fresh leaves are 'cilantro' while seeds are 'coriander' in American cooking. The dramatic change in leaf shape as the plant matures often confuses gardeners who think their cilantro has 'bolted' into a different plant entirely.
compareHints: Coriander is the only species in its genus found in New England. Among carrot family members, it's distinguished by its unique leaf progression from broad to thread-like and its distinctive smell. Unlike wild carrot or poison hemlock, coriander is much smaller and has the characteristic aromatic leaves that make identification certain.
